questions.question: The rapid switching of the CPU between processes to create the illusion of simultaneous execution is called:
questions.rationale: Context switches happen thousands of times per second, letting one core run many programs 'at once'.

questions.question: A process waiting for a disk read to finish is in which state?
questions.rationale: Blocked processes wait for an event (like I/O); they cannot use the CPU even if it is free until the event arrives.

questions.question: Why can't one misbehaving program normally corrupt another program's memory?
options: Programs share one big memory block policed by users
Each process gets an isolated virtual address space
Memory is read-only for all programs
questions.rationale: Virtual memory gives each process its own private address space, with the OS and hardware enforcing isolation.

questions.question: Which component of the OS runs in kernel mode and handles scheduling, drivers, and the memory manager?
questions.rationale: The kernel is the privileged OS core; user programs reach it only through system calls like open() or fork().

questions.question: When physical RAM fills up, the OS moves less-used pages to disk. This lets virtual memory be:
options: Larger than physical memory, at a speed cost
questions.rationale: Paging to disk extends apparent memory beyond installed RAM, but accessing disk pages is far slower than RAM.

questions.question: Which OS job is responsible for turning raw disk blocks into files and folders?
questions.rationale: The file system's job is organising raw disk blocks into files and directories — e.g., saving a document.

questions.question: A process that is waiting for its turn on the CPU (the CPU is busy elsewhere) is in which state?
questions.rationale: 'Ready' means waiting for a turn on the CPU; 'Blocked' means waiting for an event like I/O even if the CPU is free.

questions.question: What does a process consist of, beyond its code?
options: Only its file name on disk
Its current state: program counter, registers, open files, and memory
questions.rationale: A process is a running program: code plus current state — program counter, registers, open files, memory.

questions.question: Which mechanism is the doorway through which user programs request privileged work from the kernel?
options: System calls such as open(), read(), fork()
questions.rationale: User programs run with restricted rights in user mode; privileged operations happen in kernel mode via system calls like open(), read(), fork().

questions.question: File metadata typically records which of the following?
options: Size, timestamps, and permissions per file
The CPU scheduling priority of the file
The physical RAM address of the file
questions.rationale: Metadata stores size, timestamps, and permissions per file; permissions decide who may read, write, or execute.

questions.question: Linux, Windows NT, and macOS's XNU differ mainly in:
options: Their design choices (monolithic vs hybrid kernels)
Whether they support multitasking at all
questions.rationale: All three provide scheduling, memory isolation, and files — they differ mainly in design choices like monolithic vs hybrid kernels, not in fundamentals.
